questiontext.text:
Which is the best summary of the proof above that the product of any three consecutive positive integers is a multiple of 6?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A good summary names the structure of the proof and its key idea. The proof does not use the expanded product. It shows that the product has a factor 2 (one or two of the numbers are even) and a factor 3 (one of them is a multiple of 3), and combines the two. That is the second option.

  • Multiplying out was the first attempt, and the solution abandoned it (start again): \(n^3 + 3n^2 + 2n\) shows no factor of 6.

  • Checking some products gives evidence, not a proof: there are infinitely many sets of three consecutive integers.

  • Three consecutive integers need not include a multiple of 6: 7, 8 and 9 do not. Their product, \(504 = 6 \times 84\), is still a multiple of 6, because 8 is even and 9 is a multiple of 3.

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 6.2 (the product of any three consecutive positive integers is a multiple of 6), pp. 24-25, in Section 6 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Yes. The proof finds a factor 2 and a factor 3 separately, then combines them.
The solution tried this first and abandoned it (start again): \(n^3 + 3n^2 + 2n\) shows no factor of 6. Summarise the argument that came after the fresh start.
Checking some products gives evidence, not a proof: there are infinitely many sets of three consecutive integers. The proof deals with all of them at once.

falsefeedback.text: Three consecutive integers need not include a multiple of 6: 7, 8 and 9 do not, although their product, \(504 = 6 \times 84\), is a multiple of 6. So the proof cannot rest on this claim. Look again at where the proof finds its factors.
